episodes.title: Why Excel TRIM Didn't Remove That Hidden Space #Shorts
source_linked_claims: TRIM only targets ASCII 32, not NBSP 160
scenes: You cleaned a name with Excel TRIM, but the hidden space remained. It might be a nonbreaking space.
Microsoft explains that TRIM handles normal ASCII spaces, but does not remove character one sixty by itself.
In this invented row, check the character code instead of repeatedly running the same formula.
Replace character one sixty with an ordinary space using SUBSTITUTE, then wrap the result in TRIM.
Use equals TRIM, open parenthesis, SUBSTITUTE of A two, CHAR one sixty, and a space. Verify your actual data.

episodes.title: Excel Remove Duplicates Can Delete Data! Check This First #Shorts
source_linked_claims: Remove Duplicates permanently deletes; identify correct columns
scenes: Remove Duplicates can permanently delete a row. In this fictional table, one choice changes your data.
Two people can share a name. A duplicate name alone does not prove two complete records are duplicates.
Microsoft recommends highlighting duplicate values to review them before deciding what to delete.
Copy the original table to another sheet. Choose the identifying columns intentionally before removing rows.
Review the duplicates and compare row counts after cleanup. Don't delete useful records just to tidy a table.

episodes.title: Clean Messy Excel Data Without Deleting the Wrong Rows
source_linked_claims: Microsoft support remove duplicates, TRIM function, Power Query types
scenes: Here is a fictional sales table with five rows. Someone selects only the name column and removes duplicates. One entirely different customer's row disappears. The screen looks neater, but the data is now wrong.
A reliable cleanup process starts with a question: which records should exist afterward? Save a copy of the raw file, record its row count, and decide what a unique record means in that dataset.

Make a working copy and keep the raw original untouched. Microsoft cautions that Remove Duplicates permanently deletes duplicate rows from the selected range. A backup lets you undo an incorrect choice.
Visible names can look equal while hidden spaces make them different. TRIM removes excess ordinary spaces. Clean the name in a helper column first, instead of overwriting the only stored original.

One more twist: a nonbreaking space can survive TRIM because Excel's function is designed for ASCII character thirty two. Microsoft recommends checking and replacing character one sixty separately, for example with SUBSTITUTE.

Next check your data types. An identifier like zero zero one two three is a label, not a number you intend to calculate. If conversion already lost zeros, changing the display format does not reconstruct the source value.
Now highlight potential duplicates without removing them. Decide whether customer ID, order ID, or another set of columns identifies a unique row. A common name can appear on many legitimate orders.

In this fictional example, matching a customer name alone is insufficient. Matching an order identifier can be more useful, but only after checking how the source system assigns identifiers and repeated transactions.

Excel offers conditional formatting to highlight duplicates. Compare the marked rows side by side. Copy the range before using Data, Remove Duplicates, and carefully select the intended comparison columns.
After cleanup, compare starting and ending row counts. For every removed record, identify why it was truly redundant. A file with fewer rows is not automatically a file with better data quality.

For repeatable files, Power Query can apply a reviewed transformation sequence rather than manual editing each month. Validate type detection and duplicate rules before refreshing; a repeatable mistake is still a mistake.

Before sharing the final data, sample the cleaned rows against the raw source. Audit whitespace, ID types, duplicate keys, and totals. The practical habit is simple: protect the source and verify your output.
